# dctx

> The context engine for AI-assisted software development. Fewer tokens. Stable prefixes. Exact source. One policy for every workflow.

dctx 1.1.0: a Rust CLI and MCP server; Apache-2.0; offline, no telemetry. Short: https://www.dctx.internet.technology/llms-small.txt

# Why dctx exists

What problem dctx solves, the rules it follows, and why "byte-identical output" matters even if you never think about bytes.

## The problem

An AI coding assistant only knows what is in its **context window**: the text sent to the model with your request. It cannot see the rest of your project.

Most projects are too large to send whole, so tools pick pieces. Often they pick badly: whole files when one function would do, text that looks similar but is the wrong code, code as it was before your last edit, or half a function.

Each of these costs you. Models read text as **tokens** (small chunks of text, roughly a short word or part of one), and providers bill per token. The model reads every token before it answers, so more tokens also means more waiting. And answers get worse as irrelevant text piles up. The [README](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/readme/#the-core-belief-prompt-processing-efficiency) sums it up: every token in front of a model is paid for three times, to read it, again when a cache is missed, and again in attention.

## What dctx does

dctx is a command-line tool that reads your project on your machine and answers precise questions about it: where a function is defined, what calls it, what its exact source is. Each answer fits a size budget and is built from whole pieces of syntax; a piece that is too long is marked as cut, with a way to get the rest. The same question about the same code gives the same bytes every time. An assistant can run the commands itself or call them through the built-in MCP server (`dctx mcp`; MCP is a standard way for AI tools to call other tools). dctx can also pack a whole project into one structured block for a chat.

Think of photocopying random pages of a book versus using its index. dctx is the index.

### A small worked example

Run with dctx 1.1.0 on a copy of this repository's `crates/dctx-lex-go` folder. The output is real and complete.

```text
$ dctx map find Add
# dctx-lex-go find
s:tests/fixtures/basic.go#Add	fn	L43-45

$ dctx map read 's:tests/fixtures/basic.go#Add'
# dctx-lex-go read
s:tests/fixtures/basic.go#Add	fn	tests/fixtures/basic.go
func Add[T ~int](a, b T) T {
	return a
}

$ dctx map neighbors 's:tests/fixtures/basic.go#Add' --edge calls --dir in
# dctx-lex-go neighbors
calls:in:s:tests/fixtures/basic.go#main	fn	tests/fixtures/basic.go	L59
```

`find` returns a stable id, the kind of thing it is (a function) and its lines. `read` returns the exact source. `neighbors` says that `main` calls it, on line 59.

## The philosophy

The [specification](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/spec/#2-the-core-belief-prompt-processing-efficiency) turns this into five testable rules.

**Bounded.** Every map answer has a size ceiling, reserved before anything is written, and a record is never split. The budget is up to 2,000 estimated tokens (1,000 for `explain`).
*Why it matters to you:* one question cannot flood the context window and crowd out your own instructions.

**Deterministic.** The same code and the same question give the same bytes.
*Why it matters to you:* results are repeatable, and repeated prompts can be served from a cache.

**Prefix-stable.** When context is sent again across turns, bytes that did not need to change do not change.
*Why it matters to you:* this is what keeps caching working across a conversation.

**Non-redundant.** Within one session, do not resend what was already sent unless it changed. This one is still a target.

**Honest.** Every answer states its freshness, precision and provenance, and dctx never asserts what it does not know. With `--json`, the `read` above carries `"freshness":{"mode":"strict","state":"verified"}`, a `precision` block, and `more` and `next` fields for anything that did not fit. Calls it cannot resolve are listed as `unresolved`, not guessed.
*Why it matters to you:* you and your assistant can tell a fact from a guess.

The docs add a few more commitments:

- **Offline.** No telemetry, no update checks, no model calls. A release check counted zero network connections across 16 commands. Nothing leaves your machine.
- **Private by default.** A file is classified before any byte of it is read. Secret-shaped files such as `.env`, `*.pem` and `id_rsa` are listed with content omitted, with no override in v1.
- **No embeddings.** dctx does not turn code into vectors and search by similarity. It ranks by names and syntax.
- **Features must earn their place.** A feature without a measured acceptance gate is not a dctx feature.

## Why byte-identical output matters

### Prompt caching, in plain words

Much of each request to an AI model repeats the last one: system instructions, project context, earlier turns. Providers keep a cache of prompt beginnings. If the **start** of a new prompt matches a cached one exactly, byte for byte, they reuse their earlier work on that part. Cached input costs a fraction of the normal price and is processed faster.

The match must be exact, and it is checked from the beginning. Picture a reader who remembers the first fifty pages you sent earlier. Send the same fifty pages and they skip ahead. Change one word on page two, and from that word on they must read everything again, even if pages three to fifty are unchanged.

So one changed byte early in a prompt (a timestamp, a file listed in a different order, a file size) breaks the cache for everything after it.

### Prefix-stable, simply

"Prefix" means the beginning of a text. "Prefix-stable" means the beginning stays the same unless the content there really changed. Edit one file, and only the bytes from that file onward should differ.

Timestamps are the classic problem. In 1.0.0, every line of the `dctx pack` file tree carried a modification time, and file lines a size. The tree sits near the top, so merely re-saving a file (a `touch`) changed almost the whole page as far as a cache is concerned. Since 1.1.0 tree lines carry only an id. A bare `touch` leaves the output byte-identical, and an edit keeps everything before the edited file as a shared prefix. `--tree-stamps=on` brings back the old lines.

In the same folder we appended one comment line to the last file in the tree, `tests/review_lexers_a.rs`, and compared `dctx pack .` before and after:

```text
default output:      first 117,215 of 122,437 bytes unchanged
--tree-stamps=on:    first   2,151 of 123,159 bytes unchanged
```

By default about 96% of the page is still a reusable prefix. With timestamps on, almost nothing is.

### The evidence

The [stability report](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/stability/) measured map answers on 6 November 2026, on three pinned local corpora with 11 kinds of question each. **33 of 33** text answers and **33 of 33** JSON answers were byte-identical after an unrelated edit elsewhere in the project, and all were identical over five separate runs.

The report states its limits too. It measures dctx's answers, not a provider's cache hits. It ran on Linux only. The layered design that would keep context prefix-stable across a whole conversation ([SPEC §12.1](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/spec/#121-prefix-stable-tiers-target)) is still a target.

### An illustration of money and time

*Made-up numbers, not any provider's prices.* Assume:

- an agent sends the same 20,000 tokens of project context on each of 10 turns;
- normal input costs 10 units per 1,000 tokens, cached input 1 unit;
- the cache holds between turns.

If the context is byte-identical, turn one pays 200 units and the next nine pay 20 each: 380 units. If a timestamp near the top changes every turn, every turn pays 200: 2,000 units. The model also re-reads all 20,000 tokens every turn instead of reusing them, so each answer takes longer. Real ratios differ by provider; the mechanism is the same.

### Other reasons determinism matters

- **Reproducible reviews.** A colleague who runs the same command on the same code sees exactly what the assistant saw.
- **Meaningful diffs.** If saved context changes, the code changed, not a clock or a sort order.
- **Trust.** A tool whose answers shift for no reason is hard to rely on. In the spec's words, "trust is the product".

## What dctx is not

- **Not a type checker.** Call edges come from names, scopes and imports; ambiguous references are dropped.
- **Not exact token counting.** Budgets use an estimate, `ceil(2 × UTF-8 bytes / 7)`, not a model's tokenizer.
- **Not vector search or RAG.** No embeddings in the core, and the engine never calls a model.
- **Not a hosted service or a daemon.** One binary that runs when you call it. No telemetry, not even opt-out.
- **Not finished everywhere.** Linux x86_64 is the only tested platform for v1. Plain `dctx pack` is not bounded; it sends the whole project. The desktop app is a source-only preview with no download yet.

## The core belief: prompt-processing efficiency

Every token you put in front of a model is paid for three times:

- **Prefill** — the model must process every input token before it answers. You pay per token, and you wait for it.
- **Cache misses** — providers serve repeated prompt prefixes from a cache for a fraction of the price and latency. One changed byte early in a prompt throws the rest of the cache away.
- **Attention** — answers get worse as irrelevant tokens pile up.

dctx exists to send **the fewest, most relevant bytes, in an order that stays the same between turns**, so prompts are smaller, caches hit, and the model reasons over exact source instead of guesses. That is the whole philosophy, and every feature has to earn its place against it. The [specification](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/spec/#2-the-core-belief-prompt-processing-efficiency) turns it into five testable constraints — bounded, deterministic, prefix-stable, non-redundant, honest — and eight metrics.

### One engine for every way software is built

| You work by… | dctx gives you |
|---|---|
| **Hand-coding** in an unfamiliar codebase | `dctx map` outlines, symbol search and exact source reads |
| **Copy-paste** into a chat assistant | `dctx pack` — the whole project or only what changed, in one structured block |
| **Tab completion** and IDE assistants | A library facade with millisecond reads for the editor's own context budget |
| **Agents** in a terminal | Bounded, copyable, deterministic answers: five verbs, one record per line |
| **Fully automated software factories** | A specification for signed organization policy and receipts; the policy lattice is planned |

### Zero RAG defects

Chunk retrieval over embeddings fails in predictable ways: it cuts functions in half, returns different chunks for the same question, serves stale code, leaks ignored files, and hides how much it cost. dctx does not use embeddings. It answers from a lexical graph of syntax-owned spans with explicit confidence, verifies source bytes before emitting them, and reports precision and freshness. The [spec](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/spec/#3-zero-rag-defects) names ten defect classes and their intended defenses; its [roadmap](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/spec/#31-roadmap-and-acceptance-gates) distinguishes the measured baseline from planned work.

---

## Where it comes from

dctx started in **2025 as `dircontxt`, written in pure C** ([`legacy-c/`](https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx/tree/main/legacy-c)), to solve the context problem while we were still moving to an AI workflow: one command that gave a model the whole project — structured, versioned, with diffs and a strict ignore system — instead of pasting forty files. It was rewritten in Rust in 2026 and grew a privacy-first core, a template system, a plugin host, a desktop app and map mode for agents. The goal has not changed: **context, engineered.**

---

## Installation

Requires a recent stable Rust toolchain with Cargo (the workspace includes Rust 2024 crates). Linux x86_64 is the only tested platform for v1; macOS and Windows builds are untested.

### From source

```zsh
git clone https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx
cd dctx
cargo build --locked --release -p dctx-cli
./target/release/dctx-cli --version   # dctx 1.1.0 (<git sha>)
```

The package and Cargo-built executable are named **`dctx-cli`** (`dctx-cli.exe` on Windows). The help text and examples use **`dctx`**. After building, this zsh alias lets you use those examples in the current shell:

```zsh
alias dctx="$PWD/target/release/dctx-cli"
```

### Using Cargo

From the cloned repository root:

```zsh
cargo install --locked --path crates/dctx-cli
dctx-cli --version
alias dctx=dctx-cli
```

Ensure Cargo's binary directory (normally `$HOME/.cargo/bin`) is on `PATH`. This installs `dctx-cli`; the alias supplies `dctx` in the current shell. Neither command installs a package from crates.io.

Alternatively, the Unix [installer](https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx/blob/main/tools/install.sh) builds the CLI and copies it as `dctx` to `/usr/local/bin` (or `DCTX_INSTALL_DIR`). It also creates configuration, templates and ignore rules under `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/dctx` and may request sudo for the binary copy. Review it before running.

---

## Quick Start

```zsh
dctx pack .            # whole project as one structured context block on stdout
dctx pack . --clipboard  # … straight to the clipboard
dctx                   # interactive menu
```

`dctx pack` writes to stdout, the clipboard or `--output`; it creates a text export only when you request a file. Its tree lines carry the `ID` only, with no modification time and no size, so the page stays byte-identical across a bare `touch` and an edit keeps everything before the edited file as a shared prefix (what a prompt cache reuses); `--tree-stamps=on` brings back the 1.0.0 tree lines with `MOD:` and `SIZE:`. Running without arguments opens an interactive terminal menu.

---

## Map mode: context for agents

```zsh
# Run from this repository's root; map needs a file target.
dctx map map crates/dctx-cli/src/lib.rs --depth 2
dctx map find "SnapshotConfig"
# Use a stable ID returned by map/find for neighbors, explain and read.
dctx map neighbors 's:crates/dctx-cli/src/lib.rs#SnapshotConfig' --edge calls --dir in
dctx map explain 's:crates/dctx-cli/src/lib.rs#SnapshotConfig'
dctx map read 's:crates/dctx-cli/src/lib.rs#SnapshotConfig' --json
```

- **Source bytes**: `map read --json` includes source content; the current text renderer prints metadata only.
- **Bounded**: output uses an estimated token budget (up to 2,000; explain up to 1,000), not a model tokenizer guarantee, and never splits a record.
- **Deterministic**: the same tree and question give the same bytes, so prompt caches hit (see byte-stable answers below).
- **Precision and freshness**: use `--json` for the structured metadata. Structural declarations and conservative call edges do not imply exact semantic resolution.
- **Languages**: every supported language is in one of three tiers (full, outline, docs); see [Language tiers](#language-tiers) below or run `dctx languages`.
- **No Git, no network for map queries**: identity comes from dctx's own content digest; map does not need Git history or embeddings.
- **Skeleton and grep**: `dctx map skeleton <file>` prints the declaration signatures of one file, with no bodies, in source order. `dctx map grep <literal>` is an exhaustive literal search of indexed files, with hits grouped by enclosing symbol; `-i` makes it ASCII case-insensitive.
- **Hubs**: `dctx map hubs` lists the most-called symbols and the file and symbol counts per directory (`--limit` 1 to 60, default 20).
- **Path**: `dctx map path <FROM> <TO>` prints the shortest edge path (calls, imports, contains) of at most 8 hops, or `no path`.
- **Export**: `dctx map export --format json|mermaid` writes the whole graph as one deterministic document. The mermaid form is a flowchart of calls and imports. `--output PATH` writes a file.
- **Neighbors**: `--edge calls|imports` selects the edge kind, and `--depth` goes up to 4. Inbound call records carry their call-site lines, at most three per record: `\tL6,L7` in text and a `sites` array in JSON.
- **Find**: quote a multi-word concept as one argument; a name that spells the whole phrase ranks just under an exact name. For config keys with no symbol match, `find` falls back to literal hits, and a SCREAMING_CASE key (`HOME`, `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE`) always lists the code that reads it after the best exact symbol.
- **Outline of a file**: `map map <file>` lists exported top-level declarations first, then the rest in source order, with impl blocks, constants and tests last; without `--budget` its page is 1,000 tokens so `--limit 40` is not cut early. Map and find text lines are `<id>\t<kind>\tL<start>-<end>`, since the id already names the path.
- **MCP**: `dctx mcp` runs a stdio MCP server that exposes the map verbs as tools, including skeleton, path and export.
- **Byte-stable answers**: on 6 Nov 2026, build `0495f5f` preserved 33/33 text and 33/33 JSON answers after unrelated comment edits across three pinned local corpora (11 query shapes each); all were identical over five runs, with paired-answer common-prefix ratio 1.0. The tested text headers are `# <place> <verb>`; default JSON omits snapshot digest, generation and age, which `--meta` restores. [Protocol, raw answers and limits](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/stability/). Prefix-stable tier layering (SPEC §12.1) remains a target.
- **Source limit**: `DCTX_MAX_SOURCE_BYTES` sets the total source bytes one scan may read (1 to 17179869184; default 1 GiB).


Details: [Map mode guide](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/map-mode/). The three-way benchmark against graphify and Trail-Code is in [docs/BENCHMARK-20261030.md](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/benchmark/). Planned next — agent hooks, blast radius for a diff, delta answers and prefix-stable context tiers — is specified in [docs/SPEC.md](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/spec/#31-roadmap-and-acceptance-gates).

### Language tiers

`dctx languages` prints this table (`--json` for tools, `--markdown` for this block) from the one registry that also drives `dctx --version --verbose`; a test fails when the block below differs from it.

- **full**: symbols and call edges. Call edges are lexical, not type-resolved: they come from names, scopes and imports, never from a type checker, and ambiguous references are dropped.
- **outline**: symbols only; no call edges are promised. Shell function bodies can yield same-file call guesses, but v1 does not promise shell call edges.
- **docs**: headed sections.
- **Confidence**: `guess` marks the heuristic outline families, and every record from those files carries confidence `guess`; `structural` means a dedicated lexer or deterministic document rules.

| Emacs Lisp | `elisp` | `.el` | full | guess |
| JSON/JSONC/TOML/YAML | `config` | `.json`, `.jsonc`, `.toml`, `.yaml`, `.yml` | outline | structural |
| Shell | `shell` | `.sh`, `.bash`, `.zsh`, `.bats` | outline | guess |
| Makefile | `make` | `.mk`, `Makefile`, `GNUmakefile` | outline | guess |
| Dockerfile | `docker` | `Dockerfile`, `Containerfile` | outline | guess |
| Protobuf | `proto` | `.proto` | outline | guess |
| Pascal | `pascal` | `.pas`, `.pp`, `.dpr` | outline | guess |
| GraphQL | `graphql` | `.graphql`, `.gql` | outline | guess |
| Nix | `nix` | `.nix` | outline | guess |
| Markdown | `markdown` | `.md`, `.markdown` | docs | structural |
| Plain text | `text` | `.txt` | docs | structural |
| reStructuredText | `rst` | `.rst` | docs | structural |
| AsciiDoc | `asciidoc` | `.adoc`, `.asciidoc` | docs | structural |
| Org | `org` | `.org` | docs | structural |
| LaTeX | `tex` | `.tex` | docs | structural |
<!-- languages:end -->

---

## Organization control

The dctx Template System (DTS) defines output templates. The specification proposes extending it to selection, budgets, parsers, cache limits, plugins and privacy through a **seven-layer, signed policy lattice** — built-in → organization → tenant → machine → user → project → session — where each layer can only narrow the one above it. The lattice and `dctx policy explain` are planned, not current CLI commands. See [Part IV of the spec](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/spec/#part-iv--policy).

---

## Plugins

External effects are designed to run through out-of-process plugins with explicit capabilities and consent. The bundled Git plugin implements `.gitignore` protection and optional staging, but the current product host refuses native plugin launch, including the Git recipe; consent alone does not enable execution. See the [Plugins guide](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/plugins/).

```zsh
dctx plugin list
dctx plugin info dctx/git
```

---

## Security & Privacy

**The filesystem selection boundary excludes ignored file contents, including in debug mode.**

| Rule file | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `.gitignore`, `.dctxignore`, global ignore | Excluded from normal selection; `--debug-ignored` can show ignored path metadata without reading content |

Selection happens before any byte is read, hashed, parsed or cached, and is checked again before output leaves the engine.

On top of the rule files there is a strict built-in deny with no override (no flag, no `!` negation, not even `DCTX_INDEX_IGNORED=1`):

- **Sensitive files** are listed by name but never read: `.env`, `.env.*`, `*.env`, `.envrc`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.jks`, `*.keystore`, SSH private keys (`id_rsa`, `id_dsa`, `id_ecdsa`, `id_ed25519`), `credentials`, `credentials.json` and other data extensions, `*.credentials.json`, `secrets.yaml`/`.yml`/`.json`/`.toml`, `.npmrc`, `.netrc`, `.pypirc`, `.pgpass`, `.htpasswd`, `.git-credentials`. The full list is in [ADR-014](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/privacy/).
- **`.git`** at any depth is never listed or read by the map verbs, and never read by `pack`, even when a rule says `!.git/`.
- **Symlinks** are never followed: the final component is opened with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and a symlinked directory is listed by name only, never entered or read through.

dctx decides by file name only; a secret pasted into an ordinary source file is not detected. The shipped `pack`, `dctx map` and `dctx mcp` path is guarded by `crates/dctx/tests/map_sensitive_files.rs`, `crates/dctx/tests/git_and_symlink_privacy.rs`, `crates/dctx/tests/map_env_files.rs`, the unit tests in `crates/dctx/src/adapters/fs.rs`, `crates/dctx/src/domain/policy.rs` and `crates/dctx-pack/src/snapshot.rs`, and an end-to-end check that runs every command against a git-tracked canary fixture (`<repo>/scripts/checks/V1-1.zsh`).

```zsh
dctx pack . --debug-ignored  # see ignored paths in the tree without reading them
```

```gitignore
# .dctxignore
.env
.env.*
*.key
*.pem
.ssh/
secrets/
credentials/
```

The core pack/map workflows run locally, have **no telemetry**, **call no model** and **make no network calls**: the release check (`scripts/release-check.sh`) counts AF_INET/AF_INET6 connect/send calls under `strace -f` for every map verb, `pack`, `cache status` and `mcp`, and fails on any (it reports SKIP where strace cannot run). The current product CLI has no TLS network adapter for plugin discovery or downloads; network-capable distribution and plugin designs are documented separately. See the [Plugins guide](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/plugins/#what-is-not-yet-available) for current limits and [SECURITY.md](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/security/) for private vulnerability reporting.

---

## Measured, in the open

<!-- bench:begin -->
<!-- Generated by scripts/render_readme.py from docs/research/bench-3way-20261030/results/run7-53f8b6b/aggregate.json and docs/research/bench-3way-20261030/tasks/results/run5-53f8b6b/tasks_aggregate.json. Edit the script, then run it; `just readme-check` fails on drift. -->

On our 70-question protocol (designed by the dctx team; questions, gold facts and scorer are in [`docs/research/bench-3way-20261030/tasks/`](https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx/tree/main/docs/research/bench-3way-20261030/tasks)), run 31 Oct 2026 against Trail-Code 0.28.0 and graphify 0.9.97 in code-only mode, dctx scored 140/140 using 29,340 tokens; Trail-Code 122 (88,923), graphify 96 (197,203). Tokens are estimated as stdout bytes / 3.5, rounded up, for every tool.

| Tool | Points /140 | Gold facts /354 | Tokens | Tool calls |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dctx `53f8b6b` | 140 | 353 | 29,340 | 105 |
| Trail-Code 0.28.0 | 122 | 312 | 88,923 | 70 |
| graphify 0.9.97, code-only | 96 | 238 | 197,203 | 91 |

That protocol is ours, so it can favour dctx. An independently selected protocol (repositories picked by seed, callers gold from language servers, questions written without seeing dctx output) is pending: v1 card 6 publishes it, and its table will be added here whatever the result.

Cold index of the 6 benchmark corpora (flask, ripgrep, pocketbase, trailcode, mixed, docs; median of 3 runs) took dctx 0.13–1.20 s, against Trail-Code 1.04–52.83 s and graphify 4.59–59.56 s (docs: no index), on one Linux x86_64 runner (Linux 6.12.113+deb13-cloud-amd64, x86_64 CPU). Linux x86_64 is the only tested platform.

dctx makes no network calls: it made 0 socket calls in all 4 traced benchmark steps, and the release check (`scripts/release-check.sh`) asserts zero AF_INET/AF_INET6 connect/send calls under `strace -f` for every map verb, `pack`, `cache status` and `mcp`.

Raw results, corpora pins and scripts: [`docs/research/bench-3way-20261030/`](https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx/tree/main/docs/research/bench-3way-20261030); the write-up is [docs/BENCHMARK-20261030.md](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/benchmark/) (Run 7).
<!-- bench:end -->

An earlier two-way study against Trail-Code (October 2026, dctx `17dff0b`, before the call edges measured above) is in [docs/research/trail-code-2026-10](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/benchmark-oct/). See also the [changelog](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/changelog/).

---

## Out of scope for v1

- Any network or cloud feature.
- macOS and Windows support claims: they are untested; Linux x86_64 is the only tested platform.
- Watch or incremental mode beyond re-indexing.
- Shell call edges (shell is outline tier: symbols only).
- Embeddings or semantic search.
- LSP-grade type resolution: call edges are lexical.
- A stable plugin ABI or desktop API: neither is stable in v1.
- Cross-repository queries.
- Publishing to crates.io or GitHub releases (an owner decision).

---

## Open source and maintenance

dctx is open source under the [Apache-2.0](https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx/blob/main/LICENSE) license, which makes it free for any use, including commercial use. The core (`pack`) and every modality stay open, and no feature is held back behind a paid edition. Companies that depend on dctx can fund its upkeep through a [maintenance agreement](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/maintenance/), which covers security response times, long-term support and a written commitment for procurement, or through [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/Eris-Margeta). Paying never changes the license and never closes a feature. The "dctx" name and logo are trademarks of Eris Margeta; see [TRADEMARK.md](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/trademark/) for what forks may call themselves.

Project code is open source (Apache-2.0) and **ongoing work**; third-party dependencies retain their own licenses. Parts of the current development line use third-party crates; anything with third-party dependencies is not considered enterprise-ready.

The dependency policy retains the **Ed25519 signature verifier** (`ed25519-dalek`) for plugin/index verification. Signed organization policy bundles are planned; their presence in the specification does not mean the CLI can enroll or verify them today. See the [dependency policy](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/spec/#27-dependencies-and-enterprise-readiness).

---

## CLI Reference

```
Usage: dctx [PATH] [OPTIONS]
       dctx pack [PATH] [--output PATH] [--clipboard] [--json] [--tree-stamps=on|off]
       dctx pack [PATH] --for <TEXT> [--budget TOKENS]
       dctx map <map|find|neighbors|explain|read> <TARGET> [--json]
       dctx cache status|gc|purge|config|auto
       dctx template build <PATH> | template list
       dctx plugin search|install|list|info|enable|disable|remove|update|verify|run
       dctx git <status|protect>

Snapshot options:
  -c, --clipboard       Copy to clipboard
  -d, --diff            Output the diff only (if available)
  -t, --tree            Tree only (skips file content)
  -r, --reset           Force V1 reset
  --tree-stamps=on|off  MOD: and SIZE: on tree lines (default off; on = the 1.0.0 text)

Filter options:
  --ext <list>          Only these extensions, e.g. rs,toml
  --binary              Include binary files (excluded by default)
  --empty | --non-empty Only empty / non-empty files
  --large <MB> | --small <MB>
  --hidden              Only hidden files and folders
  --debug-ignored       Show ignored paths without reading them
```

Run `dctx --help` for the complete reference and `dctx --version --verbose` for feature and precision limits.

---

## Use as a library

```toml
[dependencies]
dctx = { path = "crates/dctx" }
```

This path dependency assumes your Cargo project is at this repository's root; adjust it for another location. [`crates/dctx`](https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx/tree/main/crates/dctx) is the facade used by the CLI; the desktop uses [`crates/dctx-desktop-api`](https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx/tree/main/crates/dctx-desktop-api) on top of it. Python, Node and C bindings are planned on the same facade.

## Architecture

```
dctx/
├── crates/        # Rust workspace: pure core, mode engines, adapters, lexers, plugin host, facade, CLI
├── plugins/       # First-party plugins (dctx-plugin-git)
├── apps/          # dctx-desktop
├── legacy-c/      # The original C implementation (dircontxt)
├── docs/          # Specification, design records, contracts, formal models, guides
├── presentation/  # Slides and the dctx film
├── tools/         # Benchmarks, plugin tooling, test scripts
└── website/       # dctx.internet.technology
```

Start with [docs/SPEC.md](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/spec/), then [docs/CRATE-MAP.md](https://www.dctx.internet.technology/docs/crate-map/).

# The dctx Context Management Specification

Version 1.0 · draft 2 · 21.10.2026 · Apache-2.0 · measured against
`docs/research/trail-code-2026-10` (dctx `17dff0b`, Trail-Code 0.23.1)

This document specifies **dctx**, a context engine for AI-assisted software development.
It is normative where it uses **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD** and **MAY** (RFC 2119).
Every claim it makes about the product is either marked **landed** (present in the
repository today), **contract** (a versioned contract in `docs/design/contracts/` that is
partly implemented) or **target** (specified here, not yet built), and every target
carries an acceptance gate. Nothing in this document is a marketing number: measured
values cite the pinned benchmark in `docs/research/trail-code-2026-10/REPORT.md` or the
contract that defines them.

---

  1. Purpose and the workflows served
  2. The core belief: prompt-processing efficiency

  4. Privacy and authority
- **Part II — Model**

  6. The graph: nodes, ids, outcomes
  7. Edges, confidence and provenance
  8. Precision labels
  9. Freshness
- **Part III — Answers**
  10. The verbs

- **Part IV — Policy**

  16. Organization bundles, signing and enrollment
  17. Explain and receipts
- **Part V — Index**
  18. Segments, manifests and the per-file fact store
  19. Freshness check and incremental rebuild
  20. Cold build

- **Part VI — Extension**
